planting.note: Plant in spring once frost danger has passed, siting the twining vine against a shaded trellis or wall in humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil.

directions: Lapageria rosea, the national flower of Chile, is a woody evergreen twining climber bearing large waxy, bell-shaped rose-pink (occasionally white) flowers from summer into autumn. Native to the cool, humid Valdivian rainforest understory, it demands deep shade, shelter from wind and hot sun, and constantly moist, acidic, well-drained soil to thrive. Growth is slow, often taking several years to reach flowering size, but established plants are long-lived and are traditionally trained up shaded trellises, pergolas, or tree trunks. It resents root disturbance and is usually propagated from layering or cuttings rather than transplanting mature specimens.

planting.note: Divide and transplant rooted suckers in spring into cool, moist, acidic woodland soil in deep shade.

directions: Philesia magellanica is a low, suckering evergreen shrub from the cool rainforests of southern Chile and Patagonia, closely related to Lapageria but considerably hardier and more compact. Narrow, leathery, box-like leaves set off waxy, pendant, deep rose-pink flowers produced through summer, and the plant spreads slowly by underground suckers to form a dense colony over time. It performs best in deep shade with constant moisture, acidic humus-rich soil, and cool, humid air, struggling wherever summers are hot and dry. Division of rooted suckers is the most reliable way to propagate established clumps.

planting.note: Establish divisions in spring on shaded, humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil or atop a mossy log, mimicking its rainforest habitat.

directions: Luzuriaga radicans is a creeping, wiry-stemmed evergreen native to the deep shade of Chilean and Argentine Valdivian rainforests, where it scrambles over mossy logs, rocks, and tree trunks rather than true soil. Small star-shaped white flowers appear sporadically among narrow glossy leaves and are followed by orange-red berries. It needs constant humidity, deep shade, and acidic, well-drained organic matter, making it best suited to sheltered woodland gardens in mild, moist climates. Because it roots along creeping stems, division of rooted sections is the usual propagation method.

planting.note: Divide dormant rhizomes in early spring and plant in humus-rich, moisture-retentive woodland soil in full shade.

directions: Scopolia carniolica is a clump-forming woodland perennial native to shaded forests of central and southeastern Europe, emerging early in spring with nodding, bell-shaped flowers in dusky purple-brown that appear before the foliage fully unfurls. Like its relatives belladonna and henbane, all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so it is grown strictly as an ornamental curiosity for shaded borders and woodland gardens. The foliage dies back by mid-to-late summer, so it is best paired with later-emerging shade perennials to fill the gap, and established clumps are easily increased by dividing the rhizomes in early spring or autumn. It thrives in cool, humus-rich, consistently moist soil and resents hot, dry summer conditions.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring against a shaded support in cool, acidic, moisture-retentive soil sheltered from drying wind.

directions: Berberidopsis corallina is a slow-growing, twining evergreen climber from the shaded understory of Chilean temperate rainforests, prized for its spiny-toothed, heart-shaped leaves and dangling clusters of waxy coral-red flowers produced from midsummer into autumn. It climbs by scrambling through host shrubs or over supports rather than by tendrils, so loose ties are needed when training it onto a trellis or wall in deep shade. Cool, humid air, acidic humus-rich soil, and protection from hot sun and drying wind are essential, as the roots and foliage scorch readily in exposed or alkaline sites. Propagation is typically by semi-ripe cuttings or layering, since seed is rarely produced in cultivation.

planting.note: Establish rooted cuttings in spring in warm-temperate rainforest conditions: deep shade, constant humidity, and rich, moisture-retentive soil.

directions: Berberidopsis beckleri is a rare, little-cultivated evergreen climbing shrub restricted to warm-temperate rainforest gullies on the New South Wales-Queensland border of eastern Australia, where it scrambles through the understory using twining stems. Its glossy, toothed leaves resemble those of its better-known Chilean relative Berberidopsis corallina, but its flowers are smaller and greenish-white rather than coral red. In cultivation it requires the same constant humidity, deep shade, and frost-free or near-frost-free conditions as other rainforest understory climbers, and it is grown mainly by specialist native-plant collectors rather than in general horticulture. Propagation is from cuttings, since seed is seldom available outside its native range.
sources: PlantNET - NSW Flora Online (Royal Botanic Garden Sydney)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in shaded, acidic, humus-rich soil, giving the wiry stems a shrub or wall to scramble over.

directions: Mitraria coccinea is a wiry-stemmed evergreen scrambler from the cool, wet forests of Chile and adjacent Argentina, grown for its small glossy toothed leaves and abundant bright orange-scarlet tubular flowers produced over a long summer season. It roots as it spreads, climbing by scrambling through neighboring shrubs or over rocks and logs rather than by true clinging tendrils, so it is often grown as a mounding groundcover or trained loosely onto a shaded support. Consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil and shelter from hot sun and drying wind are essential for healthy growth. It is easily propagated from semi-ripe cuttings and is a favorite of cool-climate woodland and rainforest-themed gardens.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring on a shaded mossy log or humus-rich soil, keeping roots constantly moist.

directions: Asteranthera ovata is a creeping, root-clinging evergreen from the deeply shaded Valdivian rainforests of Chile and adjacent Argentina, where it grows over mossy rocks, logs, and tree trunks much like a woodland ivy. Paired, hairy, scalloped leaves set off tubular red flowers with a white-streaked throat, produced intermittently through the warmer months. It demands near-constant humidity, deep shade, and acidic, humus-rich surfaces to root into, making it a plant for sheltered woodland or rainforest-style gardens in mild, moist climates rather than conventional borders. Cuttings taken from creeping stems root readily where humidity is maintained.

planting.note: Plant in spring in cool, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, sheltered from strong wind.

directions: Desfontainia spinosa is a dense, slow-growing evergreen shrub from the cool forests of the southern Andes and Chile, bearing glossy, spiny-toothed leaves that closely resemble holly and tubular, waxy orange-red flowers tipped with yellow through summer and autumn. It prefers the same cool, humid, acidic woodland conditions as many other Chilean rainforest understory plants, performing best in partial to full shade with constant soil moisture and shelter from drying wind and hot sun. Established plants are reasonably hardy for a Chilean rainforest native and are grown in woodland gardens across the cool, wet regions of the Pacific Northwest, British Isles, and similar maritime climates. Propagation is usually from semi-ripe cuttings taken in late summer.

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or cuttings in spring in cool, moist, acidic soil in partial shade as a creeping groundcover.

directions: Myrteola nummularia is a tiny-leaved, mat-forming evergreen groundcover native to the cool, wet moorlands and forest margins of Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego, closely related to the true myrtles. Small white or pink-flushed flowers in summer are followed by edible pink to deep red berries with a mild, myrtle-like flavor, traditionally gathered in the wild in southern South America. It roots as it creeps, forming a dense, low mat that works well tucked among rocks or at the front of a cool, moist, partially shaded border, but it struggles in hot, dry summer climates. Division of rooted sections or short cuttings in spring is the easiest way to propagate established plants.
